rationale: This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting PTSD following a medical trauma involving the near-death of a child. It excels in presenting a rich personal narrative with clear DSM criteria: traumatic exposure (Criterion A), intrusive emotional re-experiencing without clear imagery (B), extensive avoidance including emotional numbing (C), negative cognitions including self-blame and anger at the medical system (D), marked hyperarousal with hypervigilance, startle response, and reassurance-seeking (E), and significant functional impairment (G). The Ehlers & Clark elements are beautifully illustrated—fragmented memory quality, sense of current threat, specific triggers (blood, medical equipment), maladaptive strategies (thought suppression, avoidance of positive emotions), and negative appraisals about self and the world. The cultural context adds authenticity without being stereotypical.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents a comprehensive and clinically accurate portrayal of combat-related PTSD. The narrative beautifully captures the fragmented nature of trauma memory, the sense of ongoing threat ("body keeps reacting as though the danger is still present"), hypervigilance, emotional numbing, avoidance behaviors, and functional impairment. The vignette reads as a genuine personal narrative while explicitly demonstrating all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark cognitive model elements, including maladaptive coping strategies (avoidance, withdrawal) and negative appraisals (shame, self-reproach, sense of failure).

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It masterfully illustrates the Ehlers & Clark cognitive model of PTSD, showing how fragmented sensory memories (olfactory recall), negative appraisals (body cannot be trusted, self as diminished), sense of current threat, specific triggers, and maladaptive coping strategies (avoidance, distraction, covering scars) maintain the disorder. The functional impairment is clearly demonstrated through declined promotions and the freezing episode. The writing captures the phenomenology of trauma with clinical accuracy and literary quality.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents a highly realistic and clinically grounded portrayal of chronic PTSD following military-related trauma. The narrative beautifully captures all DSM-5 criteria while weaving them into a compelling personal story rather than a symptom checklist. The Ehlers & Clark cognitive model elements are richly represented—the sense of current threat (diesel smell, jackhammer triggers), negative appraisals ("world is fundamentally unsafe," survivor's guilt), fragmented sensory memory qualities (radio static, smell of diesel), and extensive avoidance/safety behaviors. The metaphor of "watching life from behind bulletproof glass" and her approach to therapy as "maintenance" rather than healing powerfully illustrates emotional numbing and avoidance strategies.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It excels in demonstrating the cognitive model of PTSD maintenance—showing how safety behaviors (exit scanning, avoidance of elevated heart rate) paradoxically maintain the sense of current threat. The vignette captures intrusion (vivid memory of the corridor), avoidance (stopping exercise, emotional numbing), negative cognitions (fear of becoming dangerous to family), hyperarousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle to nephew), and functional impairment (marital strain, occupational difficulties). The description of interoceptive triggers and the maintenance cycle is particularly sophisticated and clinically accurate.

This is a well-constructed vignette that comprehensively covers PTSD symptomatology following a natural disaster. It effectively portrays intrusion symptoms (vivid sensory memories, physical triggers), avoidance (avoiding workplace areas, not discussing trauma with family), negative cognitions (distrust, isolation, feeling disconnected), hyperarousal (sensitivity to loud noises), and clear functional impairment (work performance, social relationships). The Ehlers & Clark elements are well-represented including sense of current threat, fragmented/surreal memory quality, and specific triggers. The narrative flows naturally and feels clinically authentic. Minor weakness: some details about distrust and suspicion feel slightly elaborated beyond typical presentation.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents PTSD through a nuanced, narrative lens. It excels at depicting the sense of current threat (safety feels conditional everywhere), hypervigilance (constant exit-scanning, wariness of strangers), avoidance behaviors (avoiding exercise, pushing away positive emotions), and negative appraisals (belief that relaxation is dangerous). The trauma memory quality is subtly conveyed through how the index event "did not feel finished." Functional impairment is clearly shown in marital strain and daily life constriction. The vignette reads as authentic clinical material rather than a symptom checklist, with particularly strong depiction of safety behaviors and the cognitive-behavioral maintenance cycle.

The vignette clearly describes a traumatic earthquake event with vivid sensory re-experiencing, somatic triggers, and functional impairment at work. However, the presentation feels somewhat over-constructed with bolded terms that read more like a symptom checklist than a natural clinical narrative. The emphasis on distrust of others as a primary symptom is somewhat unusual for earthquake trauma and the absence of explicit avoidance behaviors (Criterion C) is notable. The dissociative quality of memory and sense of current threat are well-articulated from an Ehlers-Clark perspective.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine personal narrative while comprehensively illustrating PTSD phenomenology. It excels in depicting the fragmented nature of trauma memory, the sense of ongoing threat, negative self-appraisals (self-blame, belief she "deserved" to live this way), and extensive avoidance and safety behaviors. The vignette captures hyperarousal symptoms (startle response, hypervigilance, sleep disturbance), intrusion symptoms (nightmares, dissociative flashbacks, cue-triggered distress), and significant functional impairment across relationships, work, and daily life. The cognitive model elements are particularly well-represented, including the sense of current threat and maladaptive coping strategies that maintain the disorder.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It portrays an older adult male who witnessed violence, with beautifully articulated fragmented trauma memory ("scattered images and sensations"), clear hypervigilance (tracking hands, watching doors, scanning for threats), avoidance behaviors (moving away from triggers, avoiding certain customers), emotional numbing ("gone flat and empty"), and specific triggers (door slamming, babies crying, sudden movements). The cognitive appraisals about institutional failure and the sense of ongoing threat are woven naturally into the narrative. The functional impairment is subtle but present—he continues working but with significant effort and narrowed life. The vignette captures the phenomenology of PTSD with clinical authenticity.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents a highly realistic PTSD case following a terrorist attack. The narrative elegantly weaves together all DSM-5 criteria: clear traumatic exposure (Criterion A), intrusion symptoms including nightmares and flashbacks (B), extensive avoidance of crowds and reminders (C), negative cognitions about safety and detachment (D), hyperarousal with startle responses and sleep disturbance (E), and significant functional impairment including forced retirement (G). The Ehlers & Clark elements are also well-represented, including the sense of ongoing threat ("safety is no longer something he can feel"), vivid sensory memory qualities, and maladaptive coping through rigid avoidance and control behaviors. The vignette reads as a genuine personal narrative rather than a symptom checklist, with rich contextual details that enhance clinical authenticity.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting chronic PTSD following witnessed violence. It masterfully portrays the full symptom constellation: vivid intrusive memories with sensory detail (the linoleum, copper smell), extensive avoidance (service entrance, avoiding news, crowded markets), hypervigilance (scanning parking lots, noting hands and jackets), exaggerated startle response (crackers dropping), sleep disturbance, and emotional numbing ("grief calcifies"). The sense of ongoing threat ("the world feels like it is holding its breath") and the 40-year duration with continued occupational functioning despite symptoms makes this a clinically realistic portrayal of chronic PTSD with remarkable narrative depth.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It comprehensively covers DSM-5 PTSD criteria including a clear traumatic event (assault by trusted colleague), intrusion symptoms (fragmented memory, physiological reactivity to internal cues like racing heart), extensive avoidance (both behavioral and cognitive), negative cognitions (betrayal, distrust of institution), hyperarousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle), and functional impairment (work warning, marital strain). The Ehlers & Clark elements are particularly well-represented: the sense of current threat, fragmented memory quality with derealization, interoceptive triggers, and maladaptive avoidance strategies. The betrayal trauma and institutional injustice themes add clinical depth and realism.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents PTSD following a natural disaster with remarkable clinical authenticity. It excels in depicting the fragmented, dissociative quality of trauma memory (feeling like it happened to someone else, body remembering before mind), specific sensory triggers (taste of floodwater, physical sensations), and the profound sense of alienation and disconnection from others. The narrative captures avoidance behaviors, hypervigilance to bodily sensations, negative cognitions about self and others, and functional impairment in social and occupational domains—all woven naturally into a compelling personal story rather than a symptom checklist.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting PTSD following witnessed violence. It comprehensively covers all DSM criteria including clear traumatic exposure (witnessing assault), intrusion symptoms (nightmares, flashbacks at work, hypnagogic re-experiencing), avoidance (route avoidance, leaving room during violent TV), negative cognitions (shame, self-blame for freezing, feeling world is dangerous), hyperarousal (exaggerated startle, hypervigilance, sleep disturbance, irritability), and functional impairment (social withdrawal, difficulty at work). The Ehlers & Clark elements are equally well-represented with vivid sense of current threat, negative appraisals about self and world, intrusive memory qualities, clear triggers, and maladaptive coping strategies. The narrative voice is authentic and reads as genuine clinical presentation rather than a symptom checklist.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting PTSD following torture/detention. The narrative is richly detailed and deeply personal, showing rather than telling symptoms: clear Criterion A (11 days of interrogation/torture), intrusion symptoms (nightmares with sensory details - taste of rust, cold metal), avoidance (cannot discuss "the nights," left husband to avoid questions), negative cognitions (emotional numbing, detachment, photographs turned down), and hyperarousal (sleeping facing door with knife, exaggerated startle to mop bucket, hypervigilance counting elevator passengers). Functional impairment is evident in divorce, workplace difficulties, and social isolation. Specific triggers are beautifully rendered (pneumatic presses, metal cups, boots on earth, air conditioner frequency). The sense of current threat is shown through "the part of her that waits for the next blow" and the memory quality through sensory fragments rather than coherent narrative. Maladaptive strategies include avoidance and isolation. The only element not explicitly present is negative appraisals in the Ehlers & Clark sense - there's no clear catastrophic interpretation or self-blame articulated.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents a rich, immersive narrative of PTSD following a mugging. The trauma (Criterion A) is vividly depicted, and intrusion symptoms are shown through the dream of the alley becoming a hospital corridor and the scent of rain pulling them back. Avoidance is explicit (avoiding the shortcut, the back alley storage room). Negative cognitions appear in their sense of being "wound too tight" and worry about becoming a burden. Hyperarousal is extensively documented (startle to car backfires, hypervigilance, sleep disturbance, checking locks). Functional impairment is clear at work and in their relationship with Sam. The Ehlers & Clark components are all present: current threat (world feels like it could crack open), negative appraisals (losing ground, becoming a burden), fragmented memory quality (time folds, rain triggers return to alley), maladaptive strategies (avoidance, safety behaviors like the knife), and specific triggers (rain, headlights, sudden touches, dog whines).

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It explicitly describes a Criterion A trauma (rape), intrusion symptoms (frozen images surfacing, freezing in the storage room doorway), avoidance (declining social gatherings, avoiding rest/stillness), negative cognitions (guilt, shame, loss of faith, belief she deserves to suffer), and hyperarousal (chronic vigilance, interpreting silence as danger). Functional impairment is clear (marital distance, inability to work with full presence). The Ehlers & Clark components are beautifully articulated: fragmented memory ("frozen frames" rather than continuous narrative), sense of current threat (silence signals imminent danger), negative appraisals (self-blame, world is dangerous), maladaptive strategies (food restriction, avoiding rest to prevent processing), and specific triggers (silence, the storage room). The vignette demonstrates sophisticated understanding of how these maintaining factors interlock.

This vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components explicitly, including traumatic assault (Criterion A), intrusive "snapshot" memories (B), avoidance of reminders and social situations (C), guilt/shame and negative beliefs about self and world (D), hypervigilance (E), and functional impairment in work and relationships (G). The Ehlers & Clark elements are well-represented: sense of current threat, negative appraisals ("I deserve to suffer"), fragmented memory quality, maladaptive strategies (eating restriction, avoidance), and triggers (silence, delays). However, the vignette is excessively long and highly repetitive—the same concepts about maladaptive strategies, sense of threat, and guilt are restated multiple times, which detracts from clarity and clinical utility. The narrative frame is present but overwhelmed by redundant theoretical language that reads more like a case formulation than a natural clinical presentation.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents a rich, detailed narrative of a parole officer who witnessed a fatal police shooting. It explicitly covers all DSM-5 criteria: traumatic event (Criterion A - witnessing death), intrusion symptoms (Criterion B - nightmares, replaying the scene), avoidance (Criterion C - withdrawing from activities, suppressing memories), negative cognitions (Criterion D - guilt, isolation, disillusionment), hyperarousal (Criterion E - sleep disturbance, anger), and functional impairment (Criterion G - work difficulties, relationship strain). Ehlers & Clark components are also well-represented, including sense of current threat ("feeling watched"), negative appraisals (guilt about not intervening), fragmented memory quality (dreams with shifting outcomes), maladaptive strategies (suppression, withdrawal), and triggers (parolees' faces morphing into the victim). The vignette is slightly verbose with some literary flourishes that don't add clinical value, but overall it is highly instructive.

This vignette is well-structured and clearly presents PTSD symptoms with explicit connections to Ehlers & Clark cognitive model components. The traumatic event (witnessing violent assault), hypervigilance, emotional numbing, fragmented memory, specific triggers (doors, babies crying), and functional impairment at work and home are all clearly described. However, the vignette reads somewhat formulaically, with repetitive explanations of how symptoms interconnect, giving it a textbook quality rather than authentic clinical narrative. Avoidance behaviors are not explicitly described beyond withdrawal. The summary paragraph at the end is unnecessary and reinforces the didactic tone.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine personal narrative while explicitly demonstrating all DSM-5 PTSD criteria and Ehlers & Clark cognitive model components. The traumatic assault (Criterion A) leads to vivid intrusive memories triggered by cologne (B), extensive avoidance of locations and situations (C), negative beliefs about self and world safety (D), hypervigilance and scanning (E), and clear functional impairment in work and relationships (G). The vignette explicitly articulates the sense of current threat, negative appraisals ("fundamentally unsafe," "broken"), the predatory quality of fragmented memory, maladaptive avoidance strategies that maintain symptoms, and specific sensory triggers. The narrative skillfully shows how these components interact and reinforce each other, making it highly instructive for understanding PTSD maintenance mechanisms.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It explicitly describes a terrorism-related trauma (Criterion A), vivid re-experiencing with "nowness" quality ("it does not feel distant or narrated; it comes back complete"), avoidance of news and reminders, self-blame and negative cognitions, hypervigilance (scanning exits, watching people for threat), and clear functional impairment at work. The Ehlers & Clark components are richly illustrated: specific triggers (gunshots, uniforms, military talk), fragmented memory quality with present-tense intrusion, negative appraisals (self-blame), maladaptive strategies (carrying a weapon, avoidance, constant vigilance), and a pervasive sense of current threat. The narrative flow and psychological depth make this highly instructive for clinical training.

This vignette is comprehensive and well-constructed, presenting a rich personal narrative with clear PTSD symptomatology across all DSM-5 criteria. The Ehlers & Clark components are explicitly demonstrated, including specific triggers (olfactory memories, footsteps, shadows), fragmented memory recall ("lose their train of thought"), negative appraisals ("cannot rely on others"), and maladaptive strategies (avoidance, fawning, overworking). However, the vignette occasionally reads as overly didactic (e.g., explicitly labeling "fawning" and including a summary paragraph), which slightly detracts from clinical authenticity. The traumatic event (mugging without physical injury) may also be borderline for Criterion A, though the psychological impact is well-documented.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting chronic PTSD following a bombing. The narrative is rich and personal, following Mateo across twenty years with vivid sensory details. All DSM-5 criteria are explicitly present: traumatic exposure (Criterion A - witnessing bombing with injured people), intrusion symptoms (Criterion B - flashbacks triggered by smells, feeling "back on that street"), avoidance (Criterion C - avoiding news, conversations, the plaza), negative cognitions/mood (Criterion D - guilt, detachment, emotional numbing, loss of interest), hyperarousal (Criterion E - hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep problems), and functional impairment (Criterion G - relationship strain, reduced work capacity). Ehlers & Clark components are also well-represented: current threat ("low-level threat assessments," world feels "precarious"), negative appraisals (survivor guilt - "why me?"), fragmented memory quality (flashbacks feel like happening now - "he's back on that street"), maladaptive strategies (avoidance, throwing himself into work), and specific triggers (antiseptic smell, sirens, loud noises).

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that presents a nuanced case of institutional betrayal trauma. The narrative is rich with specific details: fragmented memory ("trying to grasp smoke"), explicit triggers (people misbehaving, unusual silence, phone ringing), clear hyperarousal symptoms (scanning, startle response, racing heart), avoidance behaviors (avoiding routes past police stations), and negative appraisals about institutions and trust. The vignette explicitly shows functional impairment in work, marriage, and daily life. The Ehlers & Clark components are particularly well-represented, including the sense of current threat ("constant vigilance," "impending danger"), maladaptive strategies (avoidance, pushing memories away), and specific triggers. The only minor consideration is whether the index trauma fully meets Criterion A's threshold of "death, serious injury, or sexual violence," though the threatening nature of the encounter and institutional betrayal context make this clinically compelling.

This vignette explicitly covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components, but reads more like a theoretical demonstration than a genuine clinical case. The language is overly didactic (e.g., "maladaptive strategies further perpetuate the cycle of threat and negative appraisals") and repetitive, with concepts explained multiple times. While PTSD features are clearly named and identifiable, the vignette lacks the authentic voice of a real patient and feels constructed to illustrate cognitive model components rather than to represent lived experience.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting PTSD following a child's life-threatening illness. The narrative is rich and grounded, showing rather than listing symptoms. DSM criteria are clearly present: Criterion A (witnessing son's life-threatening illness), B (nightmares of son gasping, intrusive images triggered by ambulances), C (avoids hospital district, turns off TV with sick children), D (world feels fragile, loss of trust in happiness, guilt about snapping at husband), E (hypervigilance, sleep disturbance, irritability), and G (functional impact on work and relationships). Ehlers & Clark components are also well-represented: sense of current threat ("always waiting for bad news," world feels unpredictable), negative appraisals (effort cannot protect family, any peace may be followed by disaster), fragmented memory quality (she is "back beside her son's bed" when triggered, crisis "never fully became past tense"), maladaptive strategies (avoidance, excessive checking on son), and specific triggers (ambulance sounds, phone ringing, conversations about illness).

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting PTSD following a child's life-threatening illness. The narrative is rich with sensory detail (fluorescent lights, antiseptic smell, cold vinyl chair) that grounds the trauma memory. DSM criteria are clearly present: Criterion A (threat to son's life), B (intrusive memories triggered by customer questions, auditory re-experiencing of IV pump and screaming), C (extensive avoidance of hospital, photographs, medical content), D (emotional numbing, inability to share with husband, guilt about not "moving on"), E (sleep disturbance, nightmares), and G (functional impairment at work). Ehlers & Clark components are explicit: sense of current threat ("still sitting in that vinyl chair"), fragmented sensory memory qualities, specific triggers (refrigerator hum, rubbing alcohol smell), negative appraisals ("I should be happy"), and maladaptive strategies (concealment, avoidance, leaving work early).

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine personal narrative with rich contextual detail. It explicitly demonstrates trauma memory fragmentation ("the details scatter," "the sequence dissolves"), specific triggers (slamming doors, baby's wail), hypervigilance at work, emotional numbing ("feels dead inside"), and negative appraisals about institutional failure and self-blame. The sense of current threat is clearly articulated ("as if danger is perpetually imminent"). Functional impairment is evident in deteriorating family relationships and Aroha's fear of his "absence." The only criterion not explicitly present is avoidance (Criterion C), though hypervigilance as a maladaptive strategy is well-documented.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette depicting a parole officer traumatized by police violence against him. The narrative is richly detailed with explicit DSM criteria: Criterion A (violent restraint, rifle pointed at chest), B (intrusive memories triggered by stillness and disorder), C (avoiding wellness seminars, precinct courtyard, discussing heavy cases), D (betrayal beliefs about the system, detachment from colleagues), E (hypervigilance tracking exits and hands, exaggerated startle to sounds), and G (functional impairment culminating in inability to complete an intake session). Ehlers & Clark components are also explicitly present: fragmented memory ("photograph left too long in the sun," gaps he cannot cross), sense of current threat (quiet rooms feel charged, stillness signals danger), negative appraisals (system protected its own, doubting his own perception), maladaptive strategies (avoidance, withdrawal), and specific triggers (stillness, sudden sounds, disorder). The vignette reads as a genuine personal narrative with character depth and clinical authenticity.

This vignette comprehensively covers DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components with explicit detail. The trauma (witnessing police brutality), intrusion symptoms (fragmented memory activation), avoidance (of areas and colleagues), negative cognitions (betrayal, institutional failure), hyperarousal (scanning, startle, racing heart), and functional impairment (work performance, marital distance) are all clearly present. The Ehlers & Clark elements are explicitly named and illustrated: current threat, negative appraisals, fragmented memory quality, maladaptive avoidance strategies, and specific triggers. However, the vignette reads somewhat didactically with italicized technical terms that feel instructional rather than naturalistic, reducing the narrative quality and clinical grounding. The cyclical maintenance model is well-illustrated but feels overly constructed for teaching purposes.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative with rich, specific detail. The trauma memory quality is beautifully illustrated (fragmented, sensory, "nowness" of re-experiencing, dissociative quality of feeling "unreal"). Triggers are specific and well-articulated (neck pain, physical illness, storm footage). Negative appraisals about others and belonging are explicit. Avoidance strategies (clicking away, asking coworkers to take over, withdrawing from certain projects) are clearly shown. The only DSM criterion not explicitly present is hyperarousal/reactivity (E) - while there's mention of feeling "unsettled," classic symptoms like hypervigilance, startle, sleep disturbance, or irritability are not described.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a fully realized clinical narrative rather than a symptom checklist. It explicitly demonstrates all DSM-5 criteria (Criterion A: witnessed shooting/death; B: flashbacks with full sensory immediacy; C: avoids news, TV; D: self-blame, guilt about cowardice; E: hypervigilance, scanning for exits; G: functional impairment at work). The Ehlers & Clark components are richly illustrated: fragmented sensory memory that "resists language," explicit sense of current threat ("in his nervous system, has never fully ended"), negative appraisals (self-blame about cowardice), specific triggers (uniforms, backfiring cars, metal trays), and maladaptive strategies (avoidance, rumination, carrying a weapon) with clear explanation of how these maintain the disorder. The vignette demonstrates sophisticated understanding of PTSD maintenance mechanisms.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a genuine personal narrative with rich contextual detail. The trauma (mugging with weapon) is clearly described, and all DSM criteria are explicitly present: intrusion symptoms (replaying the encounter, dreams that feel like "relived moments," bodily panic surges), avoidance (avoiding walking alone after dusk, circling parking lots), negative cognitions (embarrassment about ongoing fear, going "cold and distant"), hyperarousal (startle to door slamming, tight shoulders, clenched jaw, sleep disturbance), and functional impairment (concentration fraying at work, hands shaking before procedures). Ehlers & Clark components are also well-represented: sense of current threat ("the event does not feel finished," organizing life around safety), fragmented memory quality ("replaying in small brutal pieces," present blurring at edges), maladaptive strategies (extensive safety behaviors, avoidance), and specific triggers (sounds behind them, clients standing too close, sudden animal movements).

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that reads as a genuine clinical narrative while explicitly demonstrating all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark cognitive model components. The trauma memory is explicitly described as fragmented ("their account kept breaking apart"), with specific sensory triggers (disinfectant mixed with wet fur, stale smells) that bring back intrusive memories. Negative appraisals are clearly articulated ("the event had taken something essential from them," "they used to be a happy person but now were always miserable"). The sense of current threat is vividly portrayed through ongoing hypervigilance and the belief that "the world had changed in a permanent way." Maladaptive coping strategies are explicitly named (thought suppression, avoidance, fawning response). Functional impairment is clearly documented through relationship impact and behavioral restrictions. The vignette masterfully illustrates the maintaining cycle of PTSD symptoms.

This vignette presents a well-developed narrative of a firefighter with PTSD following exposure to war-zone bombardment. It excels at depicting hypervigilance, sense of current threat ("feeling as though there is always someone or something lurking"), negative appraisals ("heightened state of alertness was necessary for survival"), and maladaptive coping strategies (avoiding exercise, pushing away positive emotions). However, the vignette notably lacks explicit intrusion symptoms (no flashbacks or nightmares are described), which is a significant gap for a PTSD presentation. The avoidance of exercise due to fear of triggering "memories or feelings" implies but doesn't explicitly describe re-experiencing. The vignette is somewhat lengthy with some repetitive content about exit-scanning behavior.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a fully realized personal narrative grounded in realistic clinical experience with torture survivors. All DSM-5 criteria are explicitly present: Criterion A (detention and torture), B (intrusive sensory memories triggered by rain, the name Paul), C (avoidance of colors/clothes, mental distraction strategies), D (depersonalization, belief the world is dangerous, loss of identity), E (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, scanning for exits), and G (divorce, social isolation, work difficulties). Ehlers & Clark components are richly illustrated: sense of current threat ("the world is a dangerous place"), negative appraisals ("my body is no longer trustworthy," "the person I used to be is gone"), fragmented/dissociated memory quality ("feels like a story she once heard"), maladaptive strategies (thought suppression, avoidance, isolation), and specific triggers (pewter sky, rain, the name Paul, proximity from behind). The vignette is highly instructive for understanding complex PTSD presentations in refugee/torture survivor populations.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that presents a complete clinical picture through rich narrative. The traumatic event (witnessing a coworker's shooting death) is vividly described, with clear intrusion symptoms (waking at 3:14 a.m., flinching at doors, shaking when triggered by gray hoodies), avoidance (avoiding the customer service counter, not speaking about the event), negative alterations (emotional numbing, loss of interest in fishing, feeling "a cold space inside his chest"), and hyperarousal (scanning doors, startle response, sleep disturbance). Functional impairment is evident in his marriage and loss of valued activities. Triggers are specific and well-articulated (birthmarks, hoodies, automatic doors). The sense of current threat is conveyed through the "shadows that were never there before" and the ongoing hypervigilance. The fragmented memory quality is shown in his selective recall during the police statement. Maladaptive coping includes avoidance and minimization ("old men get jumpy"). The only element not explicitly present is a clear negative appraisal statement, though his minimization hints at it.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a fully realized personal narrative while explicitly demonstrating all major DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components. The trauma memory is explicitly described as fragmented ("frozen images" with "moments between them gone"), triggers are specific and sensory (the particular quality of silence), negative appraisals are clear ("she deserved it," "permanently separated from the person who had done that work"), and maladaptive strategies are shown (avoidance of the storage room, controlling eating, avoiding stillness). The sense of current threat is conveyed through her bodily response to silence as "warning" and her hypervigilant reactions to colleagues being late. Functional impairment is evident in work (supervisor's concern) and marriage (withdrawal from husband). The vignette is richly detailed without any extraneous content.

This vignette is well-constructed with a clear narrative arc, explicit PTSD symptoms, and rich contextual detail. It explicitly covers all DSM-5 criteria (traumatic assault, intrusive memories/triggers, avoidance of discussing the event, negative cognitions about betrayal and institutions, hypervigilance/startle, and functional impairment at work and in marriage). Ehlers & Clark components are also well-represented: sense of current threat (silence as trigger, anticipating danger), negative appraisals (betrayal, institutional failure), fragmented memory explicitly mentioned, avoidance as maladaptive strategy, and specific triggers identified. Minor weaknesses include some slightly contrived scenario details (the off-duty officer attack premise is somewhat convoluted) and the final paragraph reads more like a treatment plan summary than clinical presentation.

This vignette is exceptionally clear and comprehensive in describing PTSD symptoms following war zone trauma. It explicitly covers most DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components, particularly excelling in describing maladaptive coping strategies (avoiding exercise, staying near exits, pushing away positive emotions) and the sense of current threat. However, the vignette reads somewhat like a clinical formulation or teaching case rather than a genuine personal narrative - the repeated use of clinical terminology like "maladaptive strategies" and the systematic coverage of symptoms gives it a textbook quality. The nature of trauma memory (fragmentation, nowness) is not explicitly described despite mentioning vivid sensory memories.

This vignette explicitly covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components, making PTSD features highly identifiable. However, the writing is overly mechanistic and didactic, repeatedly explaining causal links between cognitive model components in a way that feels artificial rather than like a genuine clinical presentation. The constant explicit labeling of psychological mechanisms ("the fragmented memory itself, directly drove her," "negative appraisal that then amplified her scanning") reads more like a teaching exercise than a realistic patient narrative, and the circular, repetitive structure creates confusion rather than clarity.

This is an exceptionally well-crafted vignette that reads as a fully realized personal narrative with rich clinical detail. The trauma (physical assault by officers) is vividly described, and the vignette explicitly shows fragmented memory ("his mind would veer away," "left with fragments"), a sense of current threat (scanning, hypervigilance, feeling "something terrible was about to happen"), negative appraisals (institutional betrayal, "deeply unfair"), and specific triggers (quickened heartbeat, silence, sudden noises). Maladaptive strategies are clear (avoidance of stairs, withdrawal from wife, sitting in garage). Functional impairment is evident in marital strain and the grocery store incident. The vignette demonstrates how PTSD can develop from institutional violence and betrayal, making it highly instructive for clinical practice.

This vignette is comprehensive and clearly written, covering all DSM-5 criteria explicitly: sexual assault (Criterion A), flashbacks and nightmares (B), avoidance of walking alone and nighttime events (C), feeling disconnected and isolated (D), hypervigilance and sleep disturbance (E), and significant work and social impairment (G). Ehlers & Clark components are well-represented with specific triggers (footsteps, door slamming, shadows), sense of current threat (familiar places seem dangerous), and maladaptive avoidance strategies. The flashback scene explicitly describes the memory feeling like "reliving the attack in real time." This vignette clearly depicts a survivor of political violence with well-articulated PTSD symptoms including specific triggers (factory machinery sounds reminding her of captivity), nightmares, hypervigilance (flinching at sudden movements), avoidance (hiding her past from children), and functional impairment (divorce, strained relationships). The trauma memory is described as fragmented and intrusive ("both distant and immediate"). Negative appraisals are present (fear of being seen as weak). The maintenance cycle—using routine/monotony as control while remaining vulnerable to triggers—is shown but not deeply explored.

This vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria explicitly: torture as Criterion A, flashbacks and nightmares for B, avoidance of gatherings for C, emotional numbing and detachment for D, hypervigilance and startle for E, and work impairment for G. However, the presentation is somewhat generic and textbook-like, lacking the idiosyncratic detail that would make it feel like a real case. The machinery trigger is a good specific detail, but the overall narrative reads more like a symptom checklist wrapped in prose than a deeply individualized clinical portrait. Negative appraisals and maladaptive coping strategies are not explicitly shown—her journaling and church attendance are presented as adaptive rather than maintaining factors.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (explosion in operations building, witnessing death) through to current maintenance mechanisms. The choice of auditing as profession, the specific sensory triggers (diesel exhaust, construction noise, truck backfires), and the way her control strategies (immaculate spreadsheets, early arrival for seat selection) paradoxically maintain hyperarousal are all clinically illuminating. The vignette explicitly shows how she appraises her fear as "a personal failure she should have audited out of her system" — a negative appraisal that maintains distress. The fragmented, sensory nature of the trauma memory ("his boot first, then his face") and the sense of current threat (feeling unsafe in civilian life, body jolting before mind catches up) are clearly demonstrated rather than merely stated.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that reads as a genuine clinical case. The trauma (witnessing a suicide by gunshot at close range) is vividly and specifically described, and the subsequent symptom presentation is richly detailed with idiosyncratic specificity—the squeaky cart wheel, counting hands, avoiding the specific tile, the "flat, dry crack" sound memory. The sense of current threat is palpable ("he no longer trusts the safety of a Tuesday afternoon"), and maladaptive strategies (continuing to work the same register, compulsive scanning) are shown maintaining his distress. The detail about dissociation ("watching himself from across the room") and the fragmented sensory quality of the memory (the boy's face "burned into his mind") demonstrate trauma memory characteristics. Every detail serves the clinical picture.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (armed robbery) through to specific beliefs, behaviors, and maintenance mechanisms. The sensory trigger of cigarette smoke, the exaggerated startle response with Dani, the mapping of exits, and the avoidance of the walking route are all concrete and idiosyncratic. The vignette explicitly shows the disconnect between intellectual knowledge and felt sense of threat ("their body has not received any of this information"), which is a key Ehlers & Clark concept. The parallel drawn between traumatized animals and Sasha's own experience adds clinical depth. Functional impairment is shown through relationship strain, social withdrawal, and occupational impact (needing recovery time after certain cases).

This vignette excels in tracing the full maintenance cycle from trauma to belief to behavior to coping. The fragmented memory quality ("stark, disconnected pictures"), specific triggers (silence, unexpected delays), negative appraisals (self-blame, shame about body being "tainted"), and maladaptive strategies (avoiding relaxation, restrictive eating as control) are all explicitly shown with concrete detail. The connection between her faith-based identity, the assault, and her current sense of being fundamentally changed demonstrates sophisticated clinical understanding. The vignette teaches how avoidance of relaxation and rigid eating function as control strategies that paradoxically maintain hyperarousal—a maintenance mechanism trainees need to see in action.

This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing the full cognitive-behavioral maintenance cycle from trauma through negative appraisals ("I used to be happy but now I am always miserable," "I cannot rely on others") to maladaptive strategies (fawning, avoidance, magical thinking) and back to intrusive memories. The specific sensory triggers (stale coffee/tobacco smell, footsteps, keys jingling) and the detailed description of how the memory arrives fragmented and disrupts speech demonstrate sophisticated understanding of trauma memory. The vignette teaches something beyond textbook knowledge—particularly how the fawn response functions as a safety behavior and how magical thinking ("it didn't really happen") paradoxically increases intrusions. Every detail serves the clinical picture, from the veterinary setting to the dog-barking incident that precipitates help-seeking.

The vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components explicitly, with a clear traumatic event (mugging with physical injury), intrusion symptoms (smell of damp earth triggering reliving), avoidance (fear of leaving house), negative cognitions (belief they cannot rely on anyone), hypervigilance (constant scanning), and functional impairment (almost missed client meeting, work distraction). The Ehlers & Clark elements are present including current threat, negative appraisals, fragmented memory (losing the thread when explaining), maladaptive strategies (magical thinking, fawn response), and specific triggers (damp earth smell). However, the vignette reads somewhat formulaic—it explicitly labels concepts like "fawn response" and "magical thinking" rather than showing them naturally, and repeats similar content multiple times. The narrative structure is present but feels constructed rather than observed, with some generic clinical language mixed with specific details.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that demonstrates clinical sophistication. The idiosyncratic details—waking at 2:47 AM, counting ceiling tiles, the perfume trigger, the dissociative flashback during intimacy with her husband—feel observed rather than constructed. The vignette explicitly shows how her avoidance and withdrawal maintain her sense of threat and shame rather than resolving it, which is valuable for teaching maintenance cycles. Every detail serves the clinical picture.

This vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components but does so in a somewhat generic, textbook-like manner. This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing the full maintenance cycle from trauma (child's cancer diagnosis and treatment) through fragmented memory, negative appraisals (self-blame, institutional distrust), maladaptive coping (thought suppression, reassurance-seeking, emotional avoidance), and how these strategies backfire to maintain the sense of current threat. This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, demonstrating the full Ehlers & Clark maintenance cycle with remarkable clarity. This vignette excels in showing the full maintenance cycle of PTSD in an older adult with witnessed trauma. The fragmented memory ("like missing frames"), specific sensory triggers (automatic doors, crying babies, sudden movements), and the way his hypervigilance manifests in his cashier role are richly detailed and clinically grounded. The connection between his negative appraisals about failed protection/accountability and his emotional numbing ("dead inside") demonstrates sophisticated understanding of how cognitions and symptoms interact. The workplace accommodations he makes (signaling for lane switches, lingering in stockrooms) show maladaptive avoidance strategies that maintain his sense of threat. The vignette teaches something textbooks often miss: how PTSD can persist for years in someone who appears functional, and how the inability to form a coherent trauma narrative itself becomes a source of distress.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (detention and torture) through to specific beliefs ("the world is a dangerous place," "she was no longer capable"), behaviors (constant mental occupation, makeup as armor, clothing avoidance), and maintenance mechanisms (vigilance that exhausts rather than protects). The idiosyncratic details—the heavy makeup as armor, the specific avoidance of dark blue blouses and wraparound skirts, the weather-triggered absences, the dissociative quality of the memory feeling like "a film she had watched"—are clinically grounded and teach something about how PTSD presents in survivors of political violence. The vignette explicitly shows how her coping strategies (constant distraction, hypervigilance) maintain rather than relieve her symptoms, which is valuable for clinical learning.

This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing a clear line from the traumatic event (son's near-death medical emergency) through to specific beliefs ("the world is inherently dangerous"), behaviors (avoiding hospital district, scanning children for distress), and maladaptive coping (emotional detachment, avoidance of discussion). The sensory triggers are highly specific and idiosyncratic—disinfectant smell, children's coughs in her shop—and the maintenance cycle is visible: her hypervigilance in the shop exhausts her, her avoidance prevents processing, and her guilt about "missing signs" perpetuates threat appraisals. The vignette demonstrates how PTSD can persist even when the feared outcome didn't occur and the child is now thriving, which is a clinically important nuance.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that demonstrates the full Ehlers & Clark maintenance cycle with remarkable clarity. The trauma memory's fragmented nature ("trying to hold water"), the specific appraisals about institutional betrayal feeding back into triggers, and the explicit mechanism by which physiological arousal becomes self-reinforcing are all shown in action rather than merely described. The vignette teaches something a trainee could not easily get from a textbook: how moral injury and PTSD interweave when the perpetrators are colleagues within a trusted system, and how the absence of narrative closure maintains the sense of ongoing threat. Every detail — from the silence as a trigger to the stairwell paralysis that brought him to treatment — serves the clinical picture.

This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed with specific, idiosyncratic details (sleeping with keys on nightstand, scanning parking lots, the pen-grabbing incident) that ground it in realistic clinical experience. The narrative traces a clear line from trauma to symptoms to functional impairment, showing how avoidance behaviors (driving everywhere, avoiding late shifts) and hypervigilance maintain the sense of threat. All DSM criteria are explicitly present, and Ehlers & Clark components are well-demonstrated, particularly the sense of current threat ("the danger feels everywhere and nowhere") and intrusive memories during procedures. The main limitation is that while comprehensive, it teaches standard PTSD presentation rather than unexpected clinical nuance.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (typhoon, near-drowning, father's hand slipping) through to specific beliefs (he is "fundamentally different," "broken in a way that cannot be fixed"), behaviors (isolation, avoidance of storm-related content, eating alone), and somatic manifestations (neck pain as body memory, taste of salt water returning). The sensory specificity—the taste of diesel and salt, the neck craned at an unnatural angle—grounds the trauma memory in lived experience. The conference room incident shows functional impairment vividly. A trainee would learn how somatic symptoms can serve as triggers, how geographic relocation can deepen rather than resolve PTSD, and how negative self-appraisals maintain the disorder.

This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, with highly specific, idiosyncratic details (the taste of silt and gasoline, neck pain as a somatic trigger, avoidance of blue color schemes and water imagery in UX work) that ground it in lived experience. The narrative traces a clear line from trauma (flash flood in Thailand) through negative appraisals (belief that people conceal chaos, feeling fundamentally broken) to maintaining behaviors (avoidance, isolation) and shows how the somatic-intrusion-appraisal loop perpetuates distress. The vignette explicitly demonstrates fragmented, sensory-dominant memory (taste arriving before or without visual imagery), derealization/depersonalization, and functional impairment (falling behind at work, Saturday spent immobilized on bathroom floor). This teaches clinical nuance about somatic triggers and maintenance cycles that a trainee would not easily get from a textbook.

This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing a clear line from the traumatic event (car bomb) through specific triggers (drill sound, domino tiles, patient flinches) to avoidance behaviors and functional impairment (forced retirement, social withdrawal). This vignette excels at demonstrating the full Ehlers & Clark maintenance cycle with exceptional clarity: the fragmented sensory memory ("smell of dust and cordite, the shouts, the metallic taste of fear"), the sense of current threat ("danger lurked everywhere"), negative appraisals (self-blame, "convinced he could have done more"), and maladaptive strategies (rumination, weapon-carrying, news avoidance) that paradoxically maintain symptoms. This vignette excels in presenting a coherent, clinically rich narrative of PTSD following a child's critical illness. This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (robbery) through specific beliefs ("you never know what can happen next," "other people were not dependable") to behaviors (hypervigilance, avoidance, timing departures) and their maintenance. The fragmented memory quality is explicitly shown ("lost the thread," "mind seemed to break apart around the memory"), and specific sensory triggers (smell, footsteps, dusk parking lot) are named. The vignette demonstrates how avoidance and vigilance maintain the sense of current threat rather than resolving it—a key Ehlers & Clark mechanism that trainees need to see in action. Every detail serves the clinical picture, from the occupation to the specific coping behaviors.

This vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components explicitly, but suffers from excessive repetition and verbosity that dilutes clinical utility. The repetitive structure and lack of concrete, idiosyncratic details (e.g., what specifically about his dental practice, his widowhood, his Latin American background connects to his presentation) make it feel formulaic rather than observed from real clinical experience.

This vignette excels in showing the somatic encoding of trauma—the neck pain as a specific trigger that links the original bracing posture to present-day re-experiencing. Functional impairment is concrete (leaving presentations, missing stand-ups, delayed work). A particularly valuable teaching element is how the somatic symptom (neck pain) becomes both a trigger and a maintaining factor.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a coherent line from a clearly described terrorist bombing (Criterion A) through two decades of PTSD symptoms. The narrative excels at showing how symptoms manifest in this specific person's life—the drill's whine blending with post-blast ringing, sitting in his car monitoring the street before work, the shame about his startle response. The Ehlers & Clark components are vividly present: current threat ("already bracing for impact before he can remind himself where he is"), fragmented trauma memory ("dreams in fragments"), specific triggers (sudden bangs, trays crashing, news about bombings), and maladaptive strategies (constant vigilance, avoidance of downtown, monitoring exits). The vignette teaches something beyond textbook knowledge—how high-functioning professionals can maintain competence while organizing their entire lives around threat management, and how grief can strip away compensatory supports.

This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (mass shooting) through specific appraisals ("I should have done something") to maintaining behaviors (carrying a weapon, constant scanning, avoidance of community). The trauma memory is explicitly shown as fragmented and sensory ("arrives across all his senses at once," "cannot describe the event in words without the sentences breaking apart"). The maladaptive coping strategies—rumination, hypervigilance rituals, weapon-carrying as safety behavior—are shown to maintain rather than resolve the sense of threat. The functional impairment is concrete and specific (sitting frozen in his driveway, shrinking practice, social withdrawal). Every detail serves the clinical picture, from the rearranged dental chair to the specific triggers in his operatory.

This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing a clear line from trauma (convoy explosion) through fragmented memory, negative appraisals (self-blame, belief she is inherently flawed), to maintaining behaviors (hypervigilance, scanning, avoidance) that paradoxically intensify both the sense of threat and the memory fragmentation. The specific triggers (cologne, loud bangs, door slams), the idiosyncratic detail of her auditor role becoming exhausting due to constant threat assessment, and the explicit maintenance cycle where checking increases perceived danger are all clinically rich. The vignette demonstrates how safety behaviors backfire—a key Ehlers & Clark insight that trainees need to see in action.

This vignette presents a coherent narrative of PTSD following a natural disaster with clear DSM criteria including traumatic exposure (typhoon), intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance (canceling social plans), hyperarousal (vigilance, startle response, sleep disturbance), and functional impairment (work difficulties). The working late as distraction qualifies as a maladaptive strategy, and triggers are identified (loud noises), but the deeper maintenance mechanisms are not illuminated.

This vignette excels at demonstrating the maintenance cycle central to Ehlers & Clark's model. The specific detail of how exit-scanning reinforces threat perception, how exercise avoidance due to interoceptive triggers increases vulnerability, and how emotional numbing damages relationships creates a coherent clinical picture. The vignette explicitly shows how maladaptive coping strategies (positioning near exits, avoiding exercise, suppressing positive emotions) paradoxically maintain and intensify PTSD symptoms rather than providing relief—a nuance that trainees need to see in action. Specific triggers (elevated heart rate, strangers approaching, ambient sounds) are clearly linked to the original trauma memory of the ambush.

This vignette excels in showing the full mechanism of PTSD maintenance. The dissociation between cognitive rejection ("the memories did not feel real") and somatic certainty ("his body remembered with absolute clarity") beautifully illustrates fragmented trauma memory. Functional impairment is concrete and escalating (working from home, manager's concerns, missing entire workdays). The vignette teaches something textbooks often miss: how the body's memory can feel more real than cognitive memory, and how this disconnect itself becomes distressing.

This vignette is highly explicit in naming DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components, with clear descriptions of the traumatic event, intrusions triggered by sensory cues, avoidance behaviors, negative cognitions about self and others, hypervigilance, and functional impairment. This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (witnessing civilian deaths during shelling) through specific beliefs ("danger could arrive without warning," "feeling good was a kind of vulnerability") to concrete behaviors (exit-scanning, avoiding exercise, pushing away positive emotions) and their maintenance effects. The vignette excels at showing how James's coping strategies backfire—avoiding exercise because elevated heart rate triggers terror, suppressing positive emotions to "stay prepared"—demonstrating the Ehlers & Clark maintenance cycle in action. This vignette excels in presenting a coherent, clinically rich narrative of PTSD following a mugging. This is an exceptionally well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from trauma (earthquake with death and injury) through to specific triggers (neck tension, disaster-related conversation), fragmented memory quality (taste without image, atmosphere rather than narrative), negative appraisals (world as performance, people as unknowable and unreliable), avoidance behaviors (gym, social events), and functional impairment (leaving a work presentation, relationship deterioration). This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing a clear line from the index trauma (torture by soldiers) through to specific beliefs ("the world is fundamentally dangerous," "she could no longer trust" her body), idiosyncratic triggers (the coworker's name Samuel, August humidity, yellow clothing), and maladaptive coping strategies (constant podcasts, heavy makeup as "armor," avoidance of church and promotion) that maintain her PTSD. This vignette excels in showing the full maintenance cycle of PTSD: the trauma (knifepoint mugging), the intrusive sensory memories (exhaust, damp concrete), the negative appraisals ("You have to be especially careful," "other people could not be trusted"), and how maladaptive coping strategies (hypervigilance, over-compliance, minimization) paradoxically maintain the disorder. This vignette is exceptionally well-constructed, tracing a clear line from trauma (rape by someone she helped) through specific beliefs (body is "stained," she deserves to suffer, happiness was "stolen permanently") to behaviors (food restriction, refusing rest, avoidance of church) and their maintenance function (hunger provides illusion of control, vigilance feels protective).
